question: Which statement best describes Client-Side Rendering (CSR)?
options: The server sends a near-empty HTML shell plus JavaScript; the browser then fetches data and renders in the client. It's flexible and cheap to host, but the user sees a blank/loading state first and SEO suffers because crawlers may see little content. Good for private, highly interactive dashboards behind auth.

Next renders the page to HTML on the server on every request, so the user gets fully-formed, data-filled HTML immediately and crawlers see real content. The trade-off is a slower TTFB (the server does work per request) and you need a running server. Use it for personalized or always-fresh pages.

Pages are rendered to HTML once at build time and served from a CDN, giving the fastest possible TTFB and great SEO. The catch is the content is frozen until the next build, so it's ideal for content that rarely changes — marketing pages, docs, blog posts.

ISR is SSG plus a refresh interval: pages are served statically but regenerated in the background after a set time (or on demand), so you get static speed with eventually-fresh data. It's the sweet spot for content that changes occasionally, like a product catalog.

question: Which statement best describes Server-Side Rendering (SSR)?
options: Pages are rendered to HTML once at build time and served from a CDN, giving the fastest possible TTFB and great SEO. The catch is the content is frozen until the next build, so it's ideal for content that rarely changes — marketing pages, docs, blog posts.

ISR is SSG plus a refresh interval: pages are served statically but regenerated in the background after a set time (or on demand), so you get static speed with eventually-fresh data. It's the sweet spot for content that changes occasionally, like a product catalog.

Server rendering (SSR/SSG/ISR) improves time-to-first-byte and first contentful paint because HTML arrives filled in, while CSR delays content until JS runs. But HTML still needs hydration to become interactive. The goal is to send meaningful HTML fast AND keep the JS needed for interactivity small.

question: Which statement best describes Static Site Generation (SSG)?
options: Pages are rendered to HTML once at build time and served from a CDN, giving the fastest possible TTFB and great SEO. The catch is the content is frozen until the next build, so it's ideal for content that rarely changes — marketing pages, docs, blog posts.

Server rendering (SSR/SSG/ISR) improves time-to-first-byte and first contentful paint because HTML arrives filled in, while CSR delays content until JS runs. But HTML still needs hydration to become interactive. The goal is to send meaningful HTML fast AND keep the JS needed for interactivity small.

ISR is SSG plus a refresh interval: pages are served statically but regenerated in the background after a set time (or on demand), so you get static speed with eventually-fresh data. It's the sweet spot for content that changes occasionally, like a product catalog.

The key mental split: SSG/ISR do work at BUILD time (or in the background), while SSR does work on every REQUEST and CSR does work in the BROWSER. Where the work happens determines freshness, speed, cost, and whether you need a server.
